Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tax Consultant
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event, Face Hiding: cover face with hands, Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Arjun Patel was thirty-two when the medical compound in the northern province collapsed under sustained artillery fire. He had been coordinating supply distributions when the first explosions rolled through the valley, thick plumes of smoke choking the air with the acrid bite of burning diesel and timber. He dropped into a tight crouch behind a fractured concrete pillar, his hands braced against the scorched ground, his body locked in that exact angle for hours while the rescue team shouted over the ringing in his ears. Their voices were sharp, frayed with desperation, demanding action that the collapsing ruins could no longer allow. He remembered pulling a heavy tarp over a colleague’s shoulders, then the sequence of days blurred into a single, fractured tapestry where cause and effect refused to align. He had been certain he could shield everyone from the worst of it, and when only silence answered from the deeper corridors of the ruined wing, a heavy, suffocating shame settled over him. The rule he had lived by—that the world operated on predictable cause and effect, that showing up with help would always matter—had completely shattered. He returned to Chicago three years later, the war zone’s geography replaced by quiet suburban streets and the fluorescent hum of a downtown tax consulting office. The altitude change did not alter the landscape of his mind. At first, he simply stopped looking at maps of the northern province, telling his wife, Meera, that the geographic memory was too loud. Over the next two years, the avoidance solidified into routine. He turned down Meera’s invitation to a friend’s engagement dinner, certain that stepping into a room full of celebration would be a profound mistake. He avoided his colleague’s memorial service, telling himself he was too busy, though he knew the graves and the quiet rooms would pull him under. When the breakroom microwave popped, releasing a faint whiff of burnt plastic, he would step into the hallway, certain the air carried the same chemical bite as the collapsed wing. At his desk, surrounded by quarterly filings, he discovered he could no longer hold a client’s file open without his attention fracturing. The office telephone would ring, and his entire body would hitch forward, his breath catching sharply. The dark hours stripped away the day’s routines, leaving him perched on the edge of the mattress, finding it impossible to feel safe until the first gray light touched the window. When Meera’s voice sharpened slightly during a disagreement about household logistics, he would fold his hands over his face, retreating into a rigid stillness, certain that any outward sign of distress would only multiply the chaos around him. He moved through his own life feeling set apart, as though he were reading a script in a language he no longer knew. Meera finally found the clinic after he missed a major client audit and stopped answering her calls. She sat him down, her voice steady but edged with worry, and told him they needed to understand why he was disappearing while still sitting right there. Arjun left the appointment with a card for a specialist in trauma work, his hands trembling slightly as he slipped it into his pocket. He was afraid that the silence he had built to keep the past at bay would eventually swallow his marriage and his career entirely. What he hoped for, quietly, was simply to sit through a meeting without his breath catching, to stand beside a grave without feeling his chest tighten, and to let himself sit at a dinner table without waiting for the world to break.
